result.summary: Minerva (Pallas) hears the Muses' songs and decides to punish the proud weaver Arachne. After Arachne refuses her warning, they weave rival tapestries; Minerva shows her own triumph and warning examples, Arachne shows the gods' love affairs. Minerva, unable to fault the work, tears it up and beats Arachne, who hangs herself and is turned into a spider.

scenes.title: Minerva Considers Arachne's Fame
scenes.summary: Minerva resolves to punish slights to divinity and turns to Arachne, famed for weaving though of humble birth in Lydia.
scenes.stakes: Arachne's reputation and Minerva's honour are at issue.

scenes.title: The Disguised Warning
scenes.summary: Nymphs admire Arachne's work, but she denies Pallas taught her. Pallas, as an old woman, advises her to yield, and Arachne scorns her.
scenes.stakes: Arachne risks the goddess's wrath through pride.

scenes.title: The Contest Begins
scenes.summary: Pallas reveals herself; Arachne blushes but persists. Both set up looms and weave with coloured threads.
scenes.stakes: Arachne stakes herself on a foolish victory and rushes toward destruction.

scenes.title: Pallas's Tapestry
scenes.summary: Pallas weaves her victory over Neptune for Athens and four cautionary tales of mortals punished by the gods.

scenes.title: Arachne's Tapestry
scenes.summary: Arachne weaves the gods' deceptions of mortal women so perfectly that neither Pallas nor Envy can fault it.

scenes.title: Arachne Becomes a Spider
scenes.summary: Pallas tears the web and beats Arachne, who hangs herself. Pallas spares her life but changes her into a spider.
scenes.stakes: Arachne loses her life and human form.

alias_notes.explanation: Pallas and Tritonia are epithets of the goddess Minerva, called Athena by the Greeks.

notable_quotes.reason: Minerva's curse that Arachne and her descendants will hang forever, explaining the spider.

analysis.text: Arachne's hubris in denying divine gifts and challenging a goddess brings punishment, but her flawless tapestry of divine crimes makes her sympathetic.
The tapestries show the Roman poet's ekphrasis, and Arachne's web criticises gods' abuse of power, perhaps echoing Augustan-era tensions about power.

legacy.text: The myth gave the zoological name Arachnida to spiders and their relatives.
Velázquez's painting The Spinners (c. 1657) is often read as drawing on the Arachne story.

fun_facts.text: Colophon and Phocæa were famed ancient centres of purple and dye trade, matching Arachne's father's craft.

language_notes.text: Tritonia is a title of Minerva, linked to Lake Triton or the river Triton. The Aonian maids are the Muses, whose haunt was Aonia in Boeotia.
Mæonian means Lydian; Mæonia was an old name for Lydia in Asia Minor. Arachne's name is Greek for spider.
Phocæan purple means dye made in Phocæa, an Ionian Greek city. Purple dye, made from shellfish, was costly and prestigious.
The long list of wool-working stages (carding, spinning, embroidering) shows every step of her craft. 'Instructed by Pallas' means a pupil of Minerva, goddess of weaving.
'Personates' means impersonates: Pallas takes on the role of an old woman, using false gray hair and a staff.
The old woman says age brings experience, so her advice deserves hearing. The 'thee/thou' forms are archaic singular 'you'.
'Bereft of thy understanding' means 'out of your wits'. Arachne insults the supposed old woman as senile.
Mygdonian: Lydian, from Mygdonia, a region name Ovid uses loosely for Asia Minor, where Arachne's city lay. The matrons are the local women.
Sley, woof, warp and shuttles are weaving terms: the sley (reed) beats the woof threads, carried by the shuttle, tightly across the upright warp.
Tyrian purple dye was made from shellfish at Tyre and was the most prized dye of antiquity, here boiled in a bronze vessel.
The rock of Mars is the Areopagus in Athens; Cecrops was the legendary first king. The dispute is Pallas's contest with Neptune to be the city's patron.
Neptune's gift in the contest was a horse (in other versions a salt spring) struck from rock with his trident, offered as a pledge for the city.
Rhodope and Hæmus were a Thracian king and queen who called themselves Jupiter and Juno and were turned into mountains.
Antigone, daughter of Laomedon of Troy (Ilion), boasted of her hair against Juno and was turned into a stork, here called a crane.
Cinyras' daughters were turned into temple steps after offending Juno; he clings to them in grief.
Mæonian Nymph is Arachne, whose father came from Mæonia (Lydia, in Asia Minor); 'nymph' here just means a young woman.
Jupiter took the form of Amphitryon to seduce Alcmena, the 'Tirynthian dame'; she bore Hercules. Tiryns was the Argive city linked to her family.
The 'mother of corn' is Ceres, who as a mare was taken by Neptune; 'mother of the winged horse' is Medusa, who bore Pegasus.
Liber is Bacchus, who tricked Erigone with grapes. Saturn took horse form to father the centaur Chiron.
Cytorus was a mountain in Paphlagonia famous for boxwood, so the shuttle is made of fine wood.
An 'Hecatean herb' is a magic herb associated with Hecate, goddess of witchcraft.

context_notes.text: This bracketed summary was added by the translator or editor; it is not Ovid's own text and gives away the story's outcome.
Minerva (Greek Athena, also called Pallas) is goddess of wisdom, crafts and weaving. She is quick to punish offences against the gods.
Tmolus was a mountain in Lydia known for vineyards. The Pactolus was a Lydian river famed for its golden sands.
Pallas (Minerva) had disguised herself as an old woman to urge Arachne to yield and apologise for boasting that her weaving surpassed the goddess's.
The Ægis was Pallas's protective breastplate or shield, associated with Jupiter and bearing the Gorgon's head.
The Pygmæan matron is Gerana, a Pygmy queen turned into a crane by Juno after being honoured above her.
Asterie was a Titan's daughter pursued by Jupiter as an eagle; Leda was seduced by him as a swan and bore Helen.
Neptune is the sea god (Greek Poseidon). Here he takes bull form to seduce Canace, Æolus's daughter.
Pallas is Minerva, goddess of weaving and wisdom, so her failure to find fault shows Arachne's skill.

literary_notes.text: Ovid introduces Arachne as famous for talent alone, not rank. This sets up her pride in skill and her clash with a goddess.
Arachne's denial of her teacher and her challenge anticipate the contest and her ruin.
Arachne boasts she will bear any penalty, unaware she speaks to Minerva herself and will indeed suffer a terrible one.
Arachne demands that the goddess come in person, not knowing she is already present in disguise.
Arachne's shifting blush is compared to the dawn sky turning purple then white, giving the shame a delicate natural image.
Her rush toward 'destruction' signals the tragic outcome of the contest before it is woven.
The rainbow comparison shows how seamlessly the colors blend, while extremes remain distinct, conveying the weavers' skill.
Pallas's warning tapestry of punished mortals is meant to teach Arachne, yet its message of divine anger will be ignored and fulfilled.
The olive, Pallas's own tree, frames the work as peace and her own authority, ending with her victory.
The claim that the bull and sea look real exaggerates Arachne's skill, establishing her art as lifelike.
Envy is treated as a person who looks for faults, making Arachne's flawless work seem beyond even jealousy.
Her high spirit shows pride and passion in Arachne, who cannot bear humiliation even from a goddess.
Her punishment keeps her weaving forever, so her talent continues in the spider's web.
